notes:
I've written notes for every verse below, but the research only goes part of the way. My tool limit ran out after a few pages, so I never reached Gill (beyond v. 1), Ellicott (beyond v. 1), Calvin, Wesley, Precept Austin, NET Bible, Bible Odyssey, or any Catholic or Orthodox site. As a result:

- **Part 2 (where Protestant traditions differ):** I didn't find any real disagreement between traditions. The writers I read are mostly older commentators, and they agree with each other. The few tradition-specific remarks I found are labelled where they come up.
- **Part 3 (other views):** I found no modern-scholarship notes, no Catholic or Orthodox readings, and no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. The only items close to it are a passing mention of end-times readings and an anti-Catholic aside from Spurgeon, both noted below.

**Overview**
- When it was written: some link the psalm to Jehoshaphat's war (2 Chronicles 20). Others think the list of ten enemies stands for the constant threat Israel lived under rather than one event.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Barnes says the only sure thing is that it was written when combined armies threatened invasion.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-83.html
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees with the Jehoshaphat date. It thinks Assyria joining such an alliance happened only once, in David's war with the Ammonites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Some see a preview of end-times alliances against Israel (Zechariah 12; Ezekiel 38).  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/83.htm

**v. 1:** It's a crisis, and God must step in if His people are to be saved. Compare the many calls for God to "arise." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the three phrases ask God not to stay a passive onlooker. They assume that when God speaks, He also acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-1.htm
- Benson (a Methodist commentator) and another older note on the same page read it as "plead for us by actions, not words." They take "hold not thy peace" as "don't be deaf" to prayers and to the enemies' insults. Same URL.
- Gill: God seems silent when He doesn't answer prayer or rebuke His people's enemies. Same URL.
- Barnes: the quick, repeated pleas show the danger was close and urgent. Same URL.
- Spurgeon (Baptist): the psalmist asks for no human leader. He rests the whole matter on God. Same URL.
- Meyer, quoted by Guzik: God has not stayed silent in the end, because the Word became flesh in Christ.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 2:** "Your enemies" means Israel's enemies are also God's. "Rage" pictures a roaring like the sea. "Reared their heads" means they took a threatening stance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Guzik: this reframing is the key point. Faith rests on God's character, not on the military odds.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Spurgeon: they boast as if they had already won. Opponents of the church tend to be noisy and boastful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-1.htm

**v. 3:** An alliance this large needed much secret plotting. "Those You cherish" (KJV "hidden ones") are the people God hides in the shelter of His presence (Ps 31:20; 27:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Matthew Henry: the world doesn't know the Lord's people, and He keeps them under special protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-1.htm
- Spurgeon pictures a hen hiding her chicks, or someone hiding a treasure from a thief.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- The Pulpit Homiletics applies "hidden ones" to Christians, whose life is "hid with Christ in God."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/83.htm

**v. 4:** Wiping Israel out was what its enemies always wanted (2 Chr 20:11; 1 Maccabees). So the verse doesn't help much with dating. Compare Exodus 17:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Guzik applies it to today: neighbouring nations and the wider world still threaten Israel.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Spurgeon: they wanted to erase Israel from history, not just kill them, because evil can't tolerate good. He adds a Protestant aside: Rome has used the same method, citing the St Bartholomew's Day massacre and the Inquisition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-1.htm
- Henry: wicked people wish all religion gone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-1.htm

**v. 5:** "Form an alliance" literally means making a covenant against God, so a formal treaty seems intended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Guzik: enemies often unite against God, as Pilate and Herod did (Luke 23:12).  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Henry: God's people are His children, so attacking them is fighting God.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_083.cfm

**v. 6:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Edom was one of Israel's bitterest and most constant enemies. 
- The Ishmaelites lived in northern Arabia and seldom appear as Israel's enemies.
- Moab was a persistent enemy.
- The Hagrites were probably a branch of the Ishmaelites, named after Hagar.
- Boice, quoted by Guzik: the Transjordan tribes fought the Hagrites.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- The Mesha Stele supports Moab's hostility.  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/83.htm

**v. 7:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Gebal is the Phoenician city (Ezekiel 27:9). The Pulpit Commentary rejects the idea of a "southern Gebal" near Edom.
- Ammon was a lifelong enemy.
- Amalek vanishes from history in Hezekiah's reign.
- Tyre was friendly early on and is first called hostile under Uzziah.
- Henry admits he doesn't know how Tyre, David's ally, ended up on this list.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_083.cfm

**v. 8:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Assyria is the climax: a great empire joining small border nations.
- The "sons of Lot" are Moab and Ammon, who seem to have led the alliance while the others helped. Guzik agrees.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Spurgeon on "Selah": the pause takes faith, because "unbelief is always in a hurry." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 9:** This recalls Gideon's victory over Midian (Judges 7–8) and Deborah and Barak's defeat of Sisera and Jabin (Judges 4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Spurgeon: faith likes to quote precedents to God, and here the nations and Israel's danger were much the same.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/83-9.htm
- Geneva Bible: these examples assured them God wouldn't let His people be wiped out.  Same URL.

**v. 10:** Judges doesn't mention Endor, but it lay near Taanach and Megiddo. "Like dung" means their bodies fertilised the soil (2 Kings 9:37). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Barnes: Endor was near Mount Tabor, and placing the battle there is reasonable.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-83.html
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik: they rotted unburied, which added to their disgrace.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 11:** Oreb and Zeeb were Midianite leaders the Ephraimites captured and killed (Judges 7:25). Zebah and Zalmunna were Midian's kings, killed by Gideon (Judges 8:21). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Spurgeon: let the ringleaders fall as well as the ordinary soldiers.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 12:** "Pastures of God" means the homesteads of God's people, Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Barnes: these are the words of the present enemies, not of the old Midianite leaders.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-83.html
- Guzik: God counts the land of Israel as His own pastures.  Kidner, quoted there, makes the same point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 13:** "Tumbleweed" (KJV "wheel") is better read as dust whirled by the wind. Both it and chaff are pictures of what is light and worthless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm

**v. 14:** May they burn away like a forest fire or brush blazing on a mountainside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm

**v. 15:** The pictures overlap, but the meaning is clear: sweep them away with the storm of God's anger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Guzik: to ancient Hebrews nothing was more powerful than a storm.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/

**v. 16:** "Shame" means their plan fails. Most of God's judgments have a merciful aim, to drive people to Him, and the psalmist shares that aim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- Guzik: God's final goal is conversion, not just destruction. Sometimes He must humble people before He saves them.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
- Henry: we should pray for our enemies' repentance, wishing them only the shame that leads to conversion.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_083.cfm
- Pulpit Homiletics, two different views on the same page:
  - Conway says Israel wanted its enemies wiped out completely, with no compromise. 
  - Another writer says Christians should see all judgment as meant to heal and correct.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/83.htm

**v. 17:** This expands the first half of v. 16 and doesn't cancel its kind wish. Like Hezekiah (Isaiah 37:20), the psalmist wants them brought low so they will know God and turn to Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm

**v. 18:** The KJV's "men" isn't in the Hebrew. It should read "that they may know." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/83.htm
- The rescue reaches outward: the aim is that the nations recognise the LORD (Ps 67:1–2).  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/83.htm
- Henry: the psalmist prays that the downfall of some will convince others.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_083.cfm
- Guzik's example: Diocletian tried to stamp out Christianity and is now forgotten, while Christ is honoured everywhere.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-83/
